links.note: In 416 or 417, Jerome's monasteries at Bethlehem were attacked and burned, and his deacon was killed. Augustine wrote that followers of Pelagius were said to have done it. Pope Innocent noted that the women who told him of it had not named the man behind it, though he saw no doubt about who was guilty. So the charge rests on report, not on a named act.

links.note: In the 350s the emperor Constantius wrote to Ezana, ruler of Aksum, about its bishop, Frumentius. In the sixth century the land still had a bishop and a Christian king. A Syriac book from soon after 525 names Euprepios as bishop under King Kaleb. Procopius calls the Ethiopian king of his day a devoted Christian, and Cosmas lists Axum as a land with churches. No bishop is named in these texts between Frumentius and Euprepios.

links.note: In 381 the Council of Constantinople, in its first canon, cursed by name the Semi-Arians, who were also called Pneumatomachi. A law of 383 banned their meetings too, as well as those of Eunomians, Arians and Macedonians. In 451 the Council of Chalcedon said the creed of 381 set out the faith on the Holy Spirit. It was aimed at those who sought to destroy the Spirit's sovereignty.
